transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-08
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood Solutions), Daniel Ortiz (CTO - MarinerIQ), Maya Chen (Head of ML), Samir Patel (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
MarinerIQ is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for a customer-facing summarization product with EU residency constraints, a strict monthly token budget, and soft latency targets around 200-400ms tail for short prompts. They want to run a pilot/benchmark to validate unit economics and latency under realistic batching patterns. Security (SOC2, KMS, audit logs) is mandatory.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, account exec on the inference team, with Priya — our systems SE — and Liam who helps with pilots. How are you all?
[00:06] Daniel Ortiz: Good, thanks. Quick background — MarinerIQ builds a regulatory summarization product for EU banks. We need EU data residency, and we have PHI-ish compliance needs for a subset of customers. Budget this year is tight, so unit-econ is a blocker.
[00:18] Alex Kim: Understood. High level, we want to map the per-token economics for hosted and what reserved/dedicated or private would look like when you factor in infra and licensing. Priya, should I pass to you for technical Qs?
[00:27] Priya Shah: Yeah, thanks. Maya, can you summarize your current traffic pattern — QPS, typical prompt length, and tail latencies you see today?
[00:33] Maya Chen: Right now we're doing ~12 QPS average, spiky to 80 during batch runs. Average prompt+response is about 800 tokens total — the input is long, like 400 tokens, response 400 — and we try to keep 95th under 500 ms but that is... we don't always hit. Also we do a lot of follow-up context so KV-cache would be nice.
[00:51] Priya Shah: Got it. So two levers we'll look at: batching behavior and caching. With continuous prefix caching / KV reuse you often see token cost reductions because you avoid recomputing prefixes; for chat like you described, that can be 20-40% effective saving depending on turn lengths.
[01:06] Samir Patel: When you say "per-token" — what's a ballpark hosted rate and how does dedicated change that? Numbers would help.
[01:11] Alex Kim: Ballpark for hosted gen — to give a working number — think in the order of tens of dollars per million tokens for base generation models for public hosted (we'll give exact in the spreadsheet). For dedicated, you commit to a monthly capacity and unit costs go down because the marginal is infra amortization — plus you can get burst pools for spiky loads. The tradeoff is commit/commitment length and predictability.
[01:28] Daniel Ortiz: When you say "tens of dollars per million" that matters a lot to run-time. Our annual budget for inference is a hard cap. We need to understand best/worst case.
[01:35] Priya Shah: Totally. For pilots we usually run a 2-week benchmark with your prompt set and traffic shape — we can show you median and tail latencies and compute a per-100k token burn. That gives a realistic unit-econ number.
[01:46] Maya Chen: Ok that helps. Also curious about quantization — can we get lower cost via 4-bit/8-bit quantized models? And does that impact latency or quality?
[01:54] Priya Shah: Yes, q4/q8 can reduce footprint and cost. On some model families quality is near-transparent, other times you see minor degradation. Latency often improves a bit because memory bandwidth is lower, but it depends on kernel profiles. We'll put model-variant suggestions in the doc.
[02:09] Liam O'Neill: Also to add, autoscaling and batching policy matters. If you allow 50-100ms make-up for batching you can get higher efficiency. But for user-facing latency SLOs around 200-400ms we design mixed policies: latency-first routes plus a lower-cost route for background jobs.
[02:23] Daniel Ortiz: The residency constraint: must store and process EU data in EU. Does Redwood support private control plane / VPC or on-prem?
[02:29] Alex Kim: Yes. Three main options: Hosted (fastest to start, model and infra in our regions — we have EU regions), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools isolated to your account, still managed), and Private (VPC or on-prem for full control). Private has higher up-front ops and licensing but meets strict residency and isolation requirements.
[02:43] Samir Patel: For private, do you offer an appliance or a package we deploy? And KMS/HSM integration?
[02:48] Priya Shah: We offer a private deployment package — can be customer VPC + private control plane or on-prem bundle. KMS integrations are supported (customer-managed keys), and we expose audit logs and RBAC for compliance. We'll include a security matrix.
[02:58] Maya Chen: Okay good. On the pricing front, hypothetical example: if we saw a 30% saving from caching and batching, would that change the dedicated vs hosted threshold?
[03:06] Alex Kim: Yes. Example: if hosted baseline is X per million tokens, and you get 30% saving via caching and batching, your effective spend is 0.7X. Dedicated pricing might be closer to 0.5X at scale after commit. So caching lowers the crossing point where hosted becomes cheaper than dedicated. We need to run your prompt set for exact curves.
[03:23] Daniel Ortiz: What about burst capacity? We have spikes during end-of-day jobs, can't have them queue.
[03:28] Priya Shah: Dedicated supports burst and pre-warmed pools. Hosted has throttles but can be configured with burst windows. Fallback routing policies can route to a lower-cost model variant if primary is saturated. We'll demo routing policies in the pilot.
[03:41] Maya Chen: Are there any hidden costs — like network egress or storage for cache?
[03:46] Liam O'Neill: For hosted, standard storage and egress apply per cloud region; we'll itemize it. KV caches are generally in-memory at runtime, so not big storage charges, but long-term retention of logs/evals is billable if you need long retention.
[03:59] Samir Patel: Regarding SLAs, if we sign dedicated with a month commit, what's the uptime SLA?
[04:04] Alex Kim: Our dedicated plans come with an SLA — typically 99.9% or higher depending on tier; private deployments have different SLA models depending on on-prem vs cloud VPC. We'll include exact SLA matrices in the pack.
[04:16] Maya Chen: We also need to validate hallucination/regression risk when moving quantized or cheaper model variants — any tooling for evals?
[04:21] Priya Shah: Yes, Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. For pilots we can run an eval harness against your golden set and report quality delta per model variant — that becomes part of the unit-econ decision.
[04:34] Daniel Ortiz: Timing — we'd like a pilot in the next three weeks if possible; budget holder needs a 2-week proof before commit. Can you do that?
[04:40] Alex Kim: Yes, timeline is feasible. We'll need your prompt set, access window for VPC peering if doing private, and a signed PoC NDA for data handling. Priya will lead the technical setup.
[04:52] Maya Chen: One more specific: do you support per-route token accounting? We need to see per-customer burn in our reporting.
[04:58] Priya Shah: Yes, token-level breakdown per API key/route is available in the console, with trace links to model versions and latency percentiles.
[05:06] Daniel Ortiz: Competitors we've looked at: we've had demos from ManagedEndpoints Co and a small EU vendor; their pricing felt opaque. We like Redwood's transparency so far.
[05:14] Alex Kim: Appreciate that. We'll be explicit in the spreadsheet with assumptions — batch sizes, average tokens per request, cache hit rates, and tail lat estimates — so you can see the sensitivity.
[05:24] Samir Patel: Operational question: if we run private and later want to move to dedicated/hosted, is migration straightforward?
[05:31] Liam O'Neill: We design for portability: same API surface, model pinning and config. Migration paths are typical: export keys and configs, then switch routing policies. There are infra specifics but we have runbooks for that.
[05:41] Maya Chen: Any blockers on our side to get started on the pilot?
[05:45] Priya Shah: We'll need the prompt set, target QPS and SLA objectives, and a test window for peering/credentials. If private pilot, we need scheduling for the infra team. NDA for data handling as Alex mentioned.
[05:57] Daniel Ortiz: Ok we'll get the prompt set and QPS numbers to you by Monday.
[06:02] Alex Kim: Great. Quick note on numbers — for planning: if you have a monthly burn cap, we'll model best/worst case with 50th/95th percentile batch sizes and cache hit scenarios. That will help procurement decide between hosted with burst, or a 6/12-month dedicated commit.
[06:18] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Also for the quality evaluation, can you include hallucination metrics and token-level alignment checks?
[06:24] Priya Shah: Yep — we'll include perplexity-like metrics, taxonomy of hallucination, and custom checks based on your golden set.
[06:30] Alex Kim: Anything else on compliance? Samir?
[06:33] Samir Patel: Just to reiterate: EU data residency, SOC2 evidence, KMS with customer-managed keys, and audit logs retention of 1 year. Also SSO/SAML for RBAC.
[06:43] Alex Kim: We'll include a one-pager mapping those items to our private and dedicated offers.
[06:47] Daniel Ortiz: Perfect. Thanks all.
[06:50] Alex Kim: We'll follow up with the pricing sheet and pilot proposal. Priya, Liam — will you take point on the technical plan?
[06:56] Priya Shah: Yep I'll own the bench and the config doc. Liam will help with runbook.
[07:01] Liam O'Neill: Yup.
[07:03] Alex Kim: Great. Thanks everyone — we'll send items over and reconvene after you share the prompt set.

End of transcript.
